newsitem.title: USA: Possible Sunday talks as UPS strike deadline looms.
newsitem.headline: Possible Sunday talks as UPS strike deadline looms.

text.p: The Teamsters Union on Saturday set a new strike deadline of midnight Sunday in its dispute with United Parcel Service, the largest U.S. package carrier.

"More than 185,000 Teamster members at United Parcel Service will go on strike on Sunday night at midnight EDT (0400 GMT on Monday) if the company refuses to agree to a new contract that provides good full-time jobs with pensions and health coverage," the union said in a statement.

Talks between the union and UPS broke off on Friday night after the first strike deadline passed at midnight on Thursday. No time was set for further negotiations, although a federal mediator said they could resume on Sunday.
"It's possible there will be sessions tomorrow," John Calhoun Wells, director of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service, told reporters on Saturday night.

Calhoun said he had just received "a comprehensive contract proposal" from the Teamsters that had been passed on to UPS. He added that it would be "unrealistic" to expect a response from the company very soon.
But a union official said it was up to the company to respond before Sunday night to avert a strike.
"We're prepared to meet up until the deadline," Teamsters spokesman Rand Wilson said.
UPS expressed interest in continuing talks, but spokeswoman Gina Ellrich called it "very unfortunate" that a new deadline had ben set.

The union said it wanted a contract that shifted more workers into full-time jobs, limited the company's ability to subcontract drivers' jobs, improved pension benefits and improved health and safety standards.
"The brown trucks won't be rolling unless this company agrees to provide the good jobs that American families need," Teamsters president Ron Carey said in a statement.
Ellrich said UPS had already offered major proposals on all of the issues, but the main sticking point appeared to be pension benefits.

"Our proposals to the union have offered more than 10,000 opportunities for part-time workers to move into full-time jobs," she said. "UPS has proposed to guarantee that no UPS driving job would be eliminated or reduced if it subcontracts."

"The issue really is pensions. UPS has offerd a programme that the Teamsters cannot live with," Ellrich said, adding that the company had made an offer that would improve workers' monthly benefits by an average of 50 percent.
UPS said it was losing about $5 million a day in business and already had begun laying off workers temporarily.
About 1 million packages each day are going to other services as the prospect of a strike grows, the company said. UPS normally delivers about 12 million packages daily.

UPS is the largest package carrier in the United States, with 1996 revenues of $22.4 billion. It handles 3.15 billion parcels and documents, shipped annually to more than 200 countries from 1,700 hubs and centres.
